title: Crushing the Anti-Sicilians | Develop Your Instincts | GM Naroditsky's DYI Speedrun

moves.spoken: With d6, Nf6, and the trades on d4 we've steered into a Najdorf — the most theory-heavy of the Sicilians.
a6 is the move that defines the Najdorf; it's the whole point of the setup.
moves.teaches: In the Najdorf, a6 fights for b5 and gives the king a future haven on c7.

moves.spoken: White's Nf3 retreat is a sideline — it withdraws the knight from the centre, so it isn't testing, but it does ask us how we want to arrange our pieces.
The key conceptual split in the Najdorf: category one pushes the pawn two squares with e5, category two plays it only one square to e6. Which you choose depends on what White commits to first.
moves.teaches: Najdorf setups divide into e5-systems and e6-systems; keep the choice open until White shows his hand.

moves.spoken: We don't need to commit the e-pawn yet, so just develop — Nc6 — and wait for White to declare himself.
e5 here simply hands over a pawn without real compensation.
We take with Nxe5, inviting the further trade — because even though the queens come off and we lose castling rights, White can't exploit it.
moves.teaches: Losing castling isn't fatal when the opponent is undeveloped and the king has a safe square waiting.

moves.spoken: The king recaptures and looks exposed, but two things save us: White is poorly developed, and the king has a ready-made home. It can simply walk to c7.

Now the point of a6 shines: it covers b5 while the f6-knight covers d5, so together they seal the light squares around the king's future home on c7. First, though, we must be ready to defend the e5-pawn once White castles and swings a rook to e1.
moves.teaches: a6 plus a knight on f6 blankets b5 and d5 — the light squares a king on c7 needs covered.

moves.spoken: Order matters: e6 first, because it opens the path for the bishop to d6, which will shield the e5-pawn against Rook-e1 pressure.
moves.teaches: Sequence your development so each move enables the defensive resource the next one needs.

moves.spoken: Kc7 parks the king on its ideal, unassailable square. Now a rook to e1 is comfortably met by Bd6.
White's f4 hopes we take, so he can come out with a bishop-check and spoil things on c7. Instead we trade on our own terms: Bd6 invites White to take on e5 rather than the other way around.
moves.teaches: Don't capture into your opponent's plan — set up the position so he has to make the trade you want.

moves.spoken: After the recapture the bishop sits beautifully in the centre, and every further trade helps us since we're the one up a pawn.
moves.teaches: When you're up material, trades bring you closer to a won endgame — welcome them.

moves.spoken: Ne4 looks scary because Nxe4 runs into the zwischenzug Bxf7-check before White recaptures on e4. But ask the real question — does White actually threaten anything right now? He doesn't, so we just carry on developing.
moves.teaches: Before reacting to a scary move, define its concrete threat; often there isn't one.

moves.spoken: So Bd7, the only clean developing move, connecting the rooks — the bishop can always reach the long diagonal later via c6.
Recapturing with the pawn, gxf6, over keeping the structure pretty — the open g-file is worth more here.
moves.teaches: A doubled-pawn recapture that opens a file for attack can beat the 'healthy' structure.

moves.spoken: The idea behind gxf6 is a slow endgame attack: the g-file plus the light bishop rerouting to c6 build a lasting threat against the g2-pawn — not mate, but relentless pressure.
moves.plans: Reroute the bishop to c6, double on the g-file, and grind the g2-pawn.

moves.spoken: No rush — Bc6 first. If White tries Bf4, it doesn't work: we take and push f5.
This is the Scandinavian/Caro-Kann pawn formation, and it's far better than it looks because every pawn defends the next. Its one real drawback is that the h7-pawn is isolated.
moves.teaches: The f5-e6 pawn chain is self-supporting; only the isolated rook-pawn is a genuine weakness.

moves.spoken: Activate the rooks starting with Rad8. With only one open file on the board, seizing it usually converts straight into material.
moves.teaches: Own the only open file and material tends to follow.

moves.spoken: A neat endgame subtlety: the natural doubling with Rg8 and Rg2 fails to Rh4, which guards the h2-pawn and keeps the king safe — so don't rush the second rook to the seventh.
moves.teaches: Calculate the 'obvious' rook lift; a quiet defensive rook shift can refute it.

moves.spoken: Why allow any counterplay when we can just snap off on b2 instead? There is no need to force the second rook in.
Under checks, tuck the king to b8 — in this endgame the rooks do the work, not the king, so keep it out of the checking lanes.
moves.teaches: In rook endings, hide the king from checks rather than marching it into activity.

moves.spoken: Simplest is to trade one pair of rooks and immediately plant the other on the open file, hitting the weak queenside pawns.
To win the b4-pawn by force, attack it from behind: Rd4 lets Rb1 defend, but starting with a check and swinging to b2 pins it down — a pawn attacked from behind can't be defended.
moves.teaches: Attack a passed or weak pawn from behind so no rook can shield it.

moves.spoken: Rely on calculation, not vague technique: use the central-kingside pawn majority to deflect White's rook off the back rank, then collect the a-pawn and make new passers.
moves.plans: Roll the kingside majority to deflect the defending rook, then win the a-pawn.

moves.spoken: The best way to defend a pawn is with another pawn — f6 props up the chain rather than tying a rook to defense.
moves.teaches: Defend with a pawn before you defend with a piece; it frees your pieces to attack.

moves.spoken: A Russian-school endgame idea worth filing away: pin the pawn laterally along the rank, then bring up your own pawn to win the f3-pawn — commonly missed even at a high level.
moves.teaches: Freeze an enemy pawn with a rook on its rank, then attack it with a pawn.

moves.spoken: This looks like a deep-freeze where one pawn holds two, but it isn't — b6 is a breakthrough. After axb6, the a-pawn runs; it's a sacrifice that costs us nothing.
moves.teaches: A pawn breakthrough sacrifices one pawn to clear the path for another to queen.

moves.spoken: In the queen-versus-pawn finish, win by zugzwang: force White to shove the h-pawn into a lost race. Kb7 is the elegant key — it makes White dig his own grave.
moves.teaches: Queen-vs-pawn endings are won by zugzwang that separates the king from its pawn.
